<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the strongest document in the series. It does what the earlier critiques asked for: a pre-registered mediation test, a second hours measure, a two-year horizon, randomised comparison, and direct engagement with both the Varga–Holm comment and the meta-analysis. Its corrections to those two papers are well founded. The arithmetic checks out.

Its weaknesses are mostly in how results are framed:

- The Summary mixes two hours measures and so overstates the decay.
- "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.
- The meetings test reuses the offices that generated the hypothesis.
- One unexamined effect, two control offices cutting their own meetings, may explain a good part of the apparent decline.

## Arithmetic checks

| Claim | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per-hour gain, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Decline on the like-for-like measure | 9.8 / 12.5 | −22%, "about a quarter" ✓ |
| Meeting-time DiD | (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) | −3.3 h, matches the 9-month figure ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |
| Halden hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden per-hour gain | 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Extra counter staff needed | 1 / 0.886 | ≈ +13%, close to the stated 12% ✓ |

One figure needs explaining. Twelve per cent more staff at the same pay would raise cost per contact by about 12% if contact volume merely returned to its old level. The stated 9% presumably assumes non-staff costs or recovered abandoned calls dilute the increase, and that assumption should be stated.

## Main problems

**1. The Summary mixes measures and overstates the decay.**
The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure. Like for like, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, a decline of 22% rather than 32%. Section 3 and Section 5 get this right ("about a quarter"); the Summary does not.

The decline is also not formally tested. The two intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 at 9 months; +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months). "Consistent with some fading" is fair. A test of the 9-to-24-month difference, run within the same model, should accompany it.

**2. The control group was contaminated, and that biases the estimated decline.**
In month 15, two control offices cut their own meetings, and their output per hour rose 4.1%. That raises the control mean and shrinks the 24-month gap between treated and control offices.

As a rough calculation, assume the other control offices didn't change. Then 2/7 × 4.1% ≈ 1.2 points. That could account for close to half the 2.7-point decline from 12.5% to 9.8%. It is a crude estimate, but it means some of the apparent fading may be the control group improving, not the treatment wearing off.

The paper treats the meeting audit only as evidence about reorganising without cutting hours. It should also report:
- a sensitivity analysis excluding the two offices;
- the per-hour gain in months 10–14, before the audit.

**3. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result.**
- **Mediation is not randomised.** Treatment was randomised; meeting time and fatigue were not. The authors note the no-confounding assumption in Limitations, but the Summary says "confirms." "Supports" would be accurate.
- **Same units.** The registered test uses the same seven treated offices that produced the exploratory correlation (r = 0.71). It is confirmatory in that it uses new time periods and a pre-specified model. It is not a replication on new units, which was the core of the Varga–Holm objection. "A larger sample of office-months" does not add independent units, because months within an office are correlated. The effective sample is still 14 clusters.
- **The intervals look too narrow.** A proportion mediated is unstable when the total effect is imprecise, and here the total effect is 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). An interval of 28–66% for the meetings share, from 14 clusters, seems narrow. The paper should state how it was computed (cluster bootstrap?) and whether the mediators were modelled jointly. Meeting time and fatigue are likely related, since fewer meetings may reduce fatigue, so the split between them depends on the model.
- **Timing.** The mediators and outcome appear to be measured over the same period. That weakens the claim that changes in the mediators came first.

**4. It is unclear what the log measure captures, and that matters for the meetings mechanism.**
"Active log-in time on the case-management system" presumably measures time spent working in the system. Meetings, phone calls and email may fall outside it. If so:
- Logs are not simply a "stricter" measure of all work. They measure a different, narrower kind of work.
- Cutting meetings would not shrink the log-hours denominator. So the 47% mediation share cannot work through "removing low-value hours." It would have to work through better focus or fewer interruptions during time in the system. That is a different mechanism from the one proposed at nine months.

The paper should say exactly what log hours include. It should also report the mediation with timesheet hours as the denominator.

**5. A reversion breaks the paper's own work-type dichotomy.**
The Summary says all three Halden reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis coding, that is discretionary work, not coverage-bound. Deadline-driven, client-responsive work may be a third category, where output isn't tied to presence but timing pressure is. This deserves discussion, not smoothing over.

## Halden subset: specific concerns

- **Missing organisations.** 14 of 23 responded. The nine non-responders may include further reversions, so the 3-in-14 reversion rate is probably an underestimate.
- **Time tracking.** Only 17 of the original 23 had both records and time tracking. Do all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking? If not, where do their actual hours come from?
- **Baseline.** The 40.3-hour baseline is identical to the 27-organisation figure in the Varga–Holm comment. Is it this subset's own baseline?
- **No control over two years.** Without a comparison group, general productivity trends over 2023–25, including new software and AI tools, are absorbed into the 11.8%. "Upper bound" is too formal a term. "Likely biased upward" is what the design supports.
- **Halden attrition is still unaddressed.** Varga–Holm reported that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the pilot began, and six cited workload. With a Halden author now on the paper, it would be the natural place to confirm or correct that account.

## Smaller points

- **Cost.** Output per employee is −3.4% at full pay, so cost per case rose by about 3.5%, plus any overtime. A county deciding whether to extend the scheme needs this figure, and the paper reports it only for the counter arm.
- **Sick days and resignations.** The sick-day figure (−27%) still isn't adjusted for fewer scheduled days, if that is how the 30-hour week was arranged. Resignations are compared as levels, not as a difference-in-differences, and have no intervals.
- **Interim results.** The follow-up protocol was registered at month 11, so months 10–11 had been seen. That is minor but should be stated.
- **Reorganisation alone.** The meeting-audit observation is suggestive. The paper rightly says it cannot settle whether reorganising without cutting hours captures the gain. A three-arm trial (hours cut / meeting audit only / control) is the obvious next study and is worth recommending explicitly.

## The responses to earlier papers

**To the Varga–Holm comment:** fair and well supported. A gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) under randomisation, record-based output, log hours and two years of follow-up is hard to call "entirely an artifact."

**To the meta-analysis:** this is a decisive correction. It shows the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so they cannot speak to decay. That bears out the concern I raised about the meta-analysis's duration claim.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Updated answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work, best evidence | About +8.5–10% at 24 months (Varden), down from 12.5% at 9 months |
| Decay | Probably modest; part of the measured decline may be control-office contamination |
| Output per worker | Small fall, about −3%; not fully offset |
| Coverage-bound work | Not viable without extra staff; the county ended this arm |
| Mechanism | Meeting cuts are a major contributor (≈ half, with caveats); fatigue is smaller; about a third is unexplained |
| Can reorganisation alone capture it? | Open; needs a three-arm trial |
| Generalisation | One public employer, seven offices per arm; private-sector evidence remains uncontrolled |

If useful, I can draft a referee report, a short note on the contamination adjustment, or update the consolidated evidence summary across all five documents.
